newsitem.title: INDIA: India says will compete with rest of Asia by 2000.
newsitem.headline: India says will compete with rest of Asia by 2000.

text.p: India said on Friday that free-trade reforms would enable it to compete with the rest of Asia by the turn of the century, but foreign analysts said New Delhi needed bolder steps to spur growth and alleviate poverty.
"India will Asianise herself and I vow that India will be as competitive as any Asian country by the year 2000," Finance Minister P. Chidambaram told a business conference in New Delhi.
"The four years thereafter, India's tariffs, tax rates and investment climate will match any other country in the world. By 2005, India will take its place in the world."

India began dismantling socialist controls on production, trade and investment in 1991. Annual growth of gross domestic product (GDP) has averaged seven percent over the past three years, above projections and the historical trend.

In his budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1, Chidambaram announced across-the-board tax cuts and some import tariff reductions which he said would align India's tax rates more closely with the rest of Asia.
The budget proposals, announced on February 28, set off a buying stampede on Indian bourses.
Chidambaram said India had attained a high growth path and aimed to raise it even further.
"We aim at sustaining seven percent growth and attaining eight percent growth at the end of the century," Chidambaram told the business conference.
The government estimates that GDP will grow by 6.8 percent in the 1996/97 fiscal year ending on March 31, and by seven percent or more in 1997/98.

Narayanan Vaghul, chairman of the Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India Ltd, said the financial services sector was ready for a "major explosion in the next two years" due to the reforms, and predicted interest rates would fall.

But several speakers at the conference said India must accelerate reforms to attain high growth and attract foreign investment needed to upgrade ailing infrastructure sectors such as power, telecommunications and ports.

"If India is to attain the growth path of seven percent and to receive $10 billion in direct investment...it appears that renewed emphasis needs to be given to the reform programme," Chulsu Kim, deputy director-general of the World Trade Organisation, said.

"The acceleration of reform would be necessary to overcome the recent slowdown of exports and industrial production, and overcome the serious infrastructure bottleneck faced by Indian companies," Kim told the conference.
Kim recommended the elimination of quantitative restrictions on consumer goods imports and a further liberalisation of the foreign investment regime.
Chidambaram said in a newspaper interview on Friday that liberalisation of consumer goods imports would help boost India's "sluggish" import growth and increase customs revenue.
Martin Feldstein, former chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under former U.S. president Ronald Reagan, said India's reforms would lead to annual economic growth of more than eight percent.
But he urged India to increase domestic savings by cutting red ink, lower trade barriers and overhaul taxes to consolidate growth.
